Oil & gas

Secure your pipelines, rights of way and gas sites from the air

A dated register of the structures inside your right of way and protection zones, each one measured to the line, with fresh digging and change between surveys flagged for your field teams. Satellite screening first, drone detail where it is needed, and a person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Send us your route file See the T-9 sample

The problem, in your words

Land along a pipeline changes between patrols

A pipeline right of way is long, narrow and mostly unwatched. What builds up inside it becomes somebody’s cost: a compensation claim, a resettlement line item, a delayed tie-in or a dispute about who was there first.

“Structures keep going up inside the protection zone.”

Each one becomes a compensation and resettlement cost if it has to move, and a harder conversation the longer it stands. You need to know where they are while they are still few.

“Our patrols don’t see what happens in between.”

Line walkers and flights cover the route on a cycle. Third-party works, new tracks and fresh digging appear between visits and are found late, if at all.

“What was there at the cut-off date?”

For a new line, a loop or a plant expansion, the land team needs a dated record of what stood in the footprint, and of what arrived after it.

“How many buildings are near the line?”

Class-location and population-density reviews need structure counts per unit length within set corridor widths, not a rough impression from a site visit.

“We can’t get to the site as often as we’d like.”

Some routes cross land where access is slow, costly or restricted. Remote screening lets the baseline start without anyone travelling.

“Our GIS has the line, not what’s around it.”

The route is in your system. The structures, clearings and tracks along it are not, and they change every season.

Rights of way and protection zones

A register of the structures inside your right of way

The core service: the structures the review confirms within the distances you choose, each measured to your line, and each stretch of route rated so your team knows where to go first.

We measure from the route you supply, in its local UTM zone, so distances are in true metres. You choose up to six bands: a statutory protection strip, your company standard, a lender’s requirement, or a wider band to see pressure building before it reaches the line. Counts are cumulative, so “within 100 m” includes everything within 50 m.

The route is then cut into 500 m stretches and each is rated for encroachment density: high where more than five structures stand inside the widest band, medium for one to five, low for none. It is a count rule that tells you where to send people first, not a safety or integrity rating. The methodology sets out every rule.

After the baseline, the same route is re-surveyed on a schedule you agree with us. New and removed structures between dated surveys are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, and your team receives a notice after each survey saying what changed and where. Fresh digging, spoil heaps, trenches and earthworks on or near the right of way are flagged in the same way, so patrols know where to look. They do not replace patrols.

What you receive

  • A structure register: ID, coordinates, distance to the line, band and chainage
  • Structure counts per unit length for your class-location reviews, with main buildings and outbuildings separated
  • An encroachment-density rating for each 500 m stretch
  • New and removed structures between dated surveys, with before-and-after views
  • A change notice after each scheduled re-survey
  • Settlement growth trends and new tracks around the line
  • Fresh excavation and earthworks near the line, flagged for checking
  • Fire-hotspot notices near above-ground installations
  • Drone checks of flagged stretches, subject to permits

New pipelines and loops

Weigh the land before the route is fixed

For a new line, a loop or a lateral, the cheapest structure to deal with is the one the route avoids. We count the structures along each alternative alignment within the same bands, so your route engineers and land team can compare options on the land they would affect, alongside their own engineering and environmental criteria.

Each option can also be screened for steep and erosion-prone stretches, drainage crossings and ground seen as water in past satellite records. Once the route is fixed, the same method gives a dated baseline of the corridor before settlement follows the new access road, and estimated households to plan consultation and the resettlement census.

The comparison is an input to route selection, not a full alternatives assessment, and the terrain work is screening, not a geotechnical or hydraulic study.

What you receive

  • Side-by-side structure counts for each alignment, by band
  • Slope, erosion and drainage-crossing screening per stretch
  • Flood-exposure screening from past satellite water records
  • A dated baseline register once the route is fixed
  • Estimated households, with the assumptions stated

LNG, gas-processing plants and field sites

Structures around plants, licence areas and resettlement villages

Around an LNG plant, a gas-processing facility or a compressor station the line becomes a boundary, and the question becomes a ring: what stands inside the site or licence area, what stands in a band around it, and what sits inside the safety and exclusion zones your engineers have drawn. We map all three, list each structure with its distance to the boundary or the source, and show how settlement around the plant, its access roads and its resettlement villages grows between surveys.

For large gas projects, the resettlement cut-off date is often the most expensive date in the schedule. A dated register of the structures in the footprint, with reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding or under construction, supports your census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5. Re-surveys of resettlement villages and buffers then show what has changed since.

During construction, dated drone orthophotos compared side by side show earthworks and laydown progress, and inventories of tanks, containers, laydown areas and heavy plant record what the imagery shows on each survey date. Detection of specific objects is tuned and checked on part of your area before it runs on the rest.

Field sites and asset handovers

A dated baseline when onshore assets change hands

When wells, flowlines and plants are sold, farmed out or handed back, the new owner inherits the land around them as well as the steel. A dated handover record fixes what stood around each well pad, flow station, flowline and plant on the day, drawn from archived imagery, a current structure register and an evidence pack, so later questions about who arrived when can be checked against the record.

At well pads and flow stations, boundary and perimeter change between dates shows new structures, cleared ground and new tracks at the edge of the site, with fence lines and gates checked by a reviewer on drone imagery.

Your own facilities are not encroachment

An operator’s plants, well pads, camps and yards are part of the asset. We record them as the operator’s installations, never as encroachment, and they stay out of the encroachment register unless you ask us to list them separately.

A handover baseline supports the new owner in later disputes. It does not decide them, and it is not a title, tenure or valuation check.

Records and events

Evidence, grievances and after the storm

Evidence and grievances

When a structure, a claim or a community concern needs a record, we package the dated imagery, the register and the maps with a manifest of file fingerprints and an independent timestamp, so you can show what was on the ground and when. The timestamp shows that the files existed at that time and have not changed since; it does not prove how the imagery was captured.

For a single point or claim, a location sheet gathers every dated image that covers it, so your grievance team can see what was there on each date. Evidence packs support legal and community processes. They do not decide claims.

After cyclones and floods

After a cyclone or flood, radar imagery maps the flooded area even under cloud, and a reviewer checks structures and assets along your route before and after the event on optical or drone imagery captured once the weather clears. Radar comparisons also show larger ground changes, such as clearing and earthworks, in months when cloud hides the ground from optical satellites.

Post-event work depends on imagery captured after the event and covers visible damage only. It is not loss adjustment or a structural assessment, and it is not an emergency service.

Satellite first, drone where needed

The right picture for each stretch

Your own imagery. If you already fly the line or buy scenes, send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs and we run the same structure, change and corridor analysis on them. Results depend on the imagery’s quality and resolution.

Archive scenes. Dated, very-high-resolution satellite scenes of your corridor, sourced from commercial archives. Coverage, dates and cloud vary by place.

A new capture. A new satellite capture requested from commercial operators when archive imagery is too old. The date depends on satellite availability and weather.

Drone surveys. Orthophotos and elevation models of the stretches that need detail, flown by Afridrone, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

Open building datasets, such as Google Open Buildings, Microsoft Building Footprints and OpenStreetMap, give a first screen across long routes and are credited in every report that uses them. See imagery and data sources for what each option can and cannot show.

Mozambique, South Africa, Nigeria

The widths and rules your register is measured against

Satellite-based surveys are available in all three countries with no site visit and no drone flight. This is a summary of public rules for orientation, as of 26 September 2026, not legal advice; the sources are linked.

Instrument What it sets
Mozambique
Lei n.º 19/97, de 1 de Outubro (Lei de Terras), arts. 8(g) and 9		 A partial protection zone of 50 m on each side of oil, gas, water, electricity and telecommunications conduits, where no land-use right (DUAT) can be acquired, only special licences
Mozambique
Lei n.º 8/2026, de 3 de Junho (Lei do Petróleo), art. 75		 A 50 m partial protection zone around petroleum infrastructure, a safety zone to be set by regulation, and compensation for crops, buildings and improvements
Mozambique
Decreto n.º 36/2001, de 20 de Novembro		 A 50 m partial protection zone and a 200 m safety zone on each side of the Pande–Temane gas pipeline corridor and around its processing plant; building there needs the operator’s prior consent
Nigeria
Oil Pipelines Act, s.12		 On the pipeline licence holder’s application, buildings and cultivation can be restricted within a set distance, up to 100 feet, of the land in the licence
South Africa
Registered servitudes		 Widths are set in each servitude agreement and diagram, so we measure to the widths your servitudes record

Português · English

Mozambique

The regulator for petroleum operations is the Instituto Nacional de Petróleo (INP). Resettlement follows Decreto n.º 31/2012, and Lei n.º 8/2026 art. 61 puts resettlement costs on the rights holder. Reports can be delivered in Portuguese for land services and district government. Drone flights are regulated by IACM, and aerial surveys also need authorisation under Lei n.º 6/2024, including for handing the survey data to you (art. 13). Where access is restricted, satellite-first work lets a baseline start without a site visit.

English

South Africa

Pipelines run in servitudes, and the vocabulary is servitude, wayleave and third-party interference. NERSA issues the licences for petroleum and piped-gas pipelines under the Petroleum Pipelines Act 60 of 2003 and the Gas Act 48 of 2001. Commercial drone work needs a UASOC and an Air Service Licence under Civil Aviation Regulations Part 101, so where you already fly your own drones we analyse that imagery. If a register is to be used as evidence about unlawful conduct, POPIA’s prior-authorisation rule (s57) may apply to your organisation: take advice first.

English

Nigeria

Upstream assets sit with NUPRC, midstream and downstream pipeline licences with NMDPRA, and Nigerian content with NCDMB. Land for pipelines can be taken under the Land Use Act (s.28), with compensation under s.29. Drone work needs an NCAA operator certificate under Nig.CARs Part 21 with security clearance built into the process, and notice to OSGOF before aerial photography for survey, so satellite screening is the practical first step. We describe this work as remote sensing and mapping of land and assets.

Moçambique (Português)Mozambique (English)South AfricaNigeria

The rules for drone flights in each country are summarised on where we work. Drone surveys are subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires, and Afridrone is working towards the operator approvals each country requires.

How it works

From route file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route and tell us what the record is for. We agree the bands, the date the record must reflect, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures are mapped along the whole route from dated imagery, open building datasets or imagery you hold.

  3. Check up close

    Drone surveys capture the stretches that need detail, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every automatic result, then each structure is measured, banded and rated, and the files are delivered.

More detail on how it works, the methodology and how we work, including tenders and supplier onboarding.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, cleared ground, fresh excavations and tracks visible from the air
  • Measure each structure to the route you supply, within the bands you set
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Deliver dated, credited records that support your land, engagement and legal processes

What we don’t do

  • Detect leaks, taps, theft, corrosion or anything about the pipe’s integrity
  • Identify, count or follow people or vehicles
  • Decide whether a structure is authorised or who is eligible for compensation
  • Replace patrols, your engineers’ class studies or your resettlement census

Frequently asked questions

Which distances can you use?

The ones that matter to you: a statutory protection strip, your company standard or a lender requirement. You can set up to six distances in one survey, and they are measured from the route file you supply (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage) or from a route we draw with you and send back for your confirmation.

How recent is the imagery, and will we know its date?

Every report names its data sources and gives the imagery dates where the source records them. We work from dated satellite scenes, drone surveys, imagery you already hold and open building datasets, which we credit and date. Where archive imagery is too old, we can request a new satellite capture; its date depends on satellite availability and weather, so it is never guaranteed. See imagery and data sources.

Can you detect leaks, illegal taps or theft?

No. We map what is visible at the surface: structures, fresh digging, spoil heaps, tracks and cleared ground. We flag it so your field teams know where to check. The pipe itself, its condition and anything underground are outside what imagery can show.

How often is the route checked?

On a schedule agreed with you. Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so this is not real-time monitoring. We re-survey the route and send a notice after each survey saying what has changed and where. How often depends on when new imagery is available, on cloud and, for drones, on permits.

Do you need access to the route or the community?

Not to start. Satellite screening needs no site access. Drone checks of flagged stretches are subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires, and ground verification stays with your teams.

Do you identify the people who live in the structures?

No. We map structures, not people, and we don’t decide whether a structure is authorised; that is for you and the authorities. Our registers support your community engagement and legal processes.

Can you support our class-location or population-density reviews?

Yes. We supply structure counts within the corridor widths and unit lengths your engineers set, with reviewer categories that separate main buildings from outbuildings. The class study and its conclusions stay with your engineers.

Who sees our route files and results?

The contacts you name. We never publish a client’s route, imagery or results without written permission, and we never publish maps of your assets or of the settlements around them. The T-9 route on this site is shown with the route owner’s permission.

Send us your route file

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, or we can draw it with you. Tell us the distances that matter and what the record is for, and we reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
